changes.after: Copy an array so its number values can change separately.

before: [3]int is an array of exactly three ints. A different length is a different array type.
Assigning one array variable to another copies its array value. A later element assignment to the copy does not mutate the original array.
Index 0 selects the first element. A runtime out-of-range index panics; it does not grow the array.
Do not transfer the copy rule to slices or pointers without examining their semantics.
Expected output or behavior: 2 9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare independent array assignment with taking a pointer later. Explain the storage involved rather than only the output. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An array holds a fixed number of items of one type. `[3]int` means exactly three integers. A different length makes a different array type.
Assigning an array to another variable copies its value. In this integer array, changing a copied item leaves the original item unchanged.
An index is an item's numbered position. Index 0 means the first item. A position outside the array is an error; it does not make the array grow.
This copying rule describes arrays. Other types, such as slices, can share the same stored items. The next lesson shows that difference.
The screen shows `2 9`. The original first item stays 2; the copied first item becomes 9.
Change only the assigned value from 9 to 7. Follow which array receives that change.

before.question: Change only the copy assignment value from 9 to 7. What prints?
choices: 7 7 because array variables always share storage.
2 7 because the array value was copied.
before.explanation: The second independent array changes while the first remains unchanged.

after.question: Change copy[0] = 9 to copy[0] = 7. What appears?
choices: 7 7, because both arrays share their items.
2 7, because the array value was copied.
after.explanation: The original first item remains 2. Only the copy's first item becomes 7.
